newsitem.title: USA: US capital securities tax status in greater peril.
newsitem.headline: US capital securities tax status in greater peril.

text.p: Wall Street will face a tough fight to preserve the tax-deductible status of newly issued capital securities and bonds with maturities longer than 40 years under the Washington budget agreement, said a top industry lobbyist.
"This will be quite an uphill battle," said Micah Green, executive vice president at the Public Securities Association (PSA) about the trade group's efforts to preserve the status quo.
"As we enter this final phase, there will be an almost insatiable need for (new) revenue to meet the instructions of the budget agreement."

Green noted that the agreement to reach a balanced federal budget by 2002 sets a general target of $85 billion in net tax cuts, consisting of $135 billion in gross tax cuts and $50 billion in revenue raising tax proposals.

Of the $50 billion in tax-cut offsets, about $30 billion is expected to come from extending the life of the airline ticket tax, leaving a $20 billion hole to be filled by miscellaneous revenue-raising measures, he said.

The Clinton Adminstration aims at saving roughly $1 billion by eliminating the tax-deductibility of capital security dividend payments and interest payments on bonds with maturities longer than 40-years, Green said.
"That is not an insignificant amount," said Green. "There are not that many similar big-ticket items to choose from."
Green said the PSA will fight to keep the tax-writing committees from eliminating the tax loophole, but he noted, "We will have our work cut out for us."
Assuming the budget resolution is passed this week, the Congressional tax writing committees could take up the issue as soon as June, he said.

Capital securities or trust preferred stock currently represent an inexpensive form of financing for banks and corporations. Issuers can deduct trust preferred dividend payments, similar to debt securities, while receiving certain benefits associated with equity financing.

Despite the bad news for issuers, spreads on the roughly $30 billion in outstanding capital securities, which would not be affected by the proposal, could tighten significantly, securities analysts said.

Andrew Gilligan, bank corporate bond analyst at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc, said the current 30-basis-point spread between most long-term bank holding company bonds and capital securities should tighten by about 10 basis points if the loophole is closed.

Gilligan said if the tax deductibility of future capital scurities was eliminated, issuers would no longer have the option of replacing their outstanding capital securities with similarly tax-advantaged securities when they become callable, usually after 10 years.
"(Outstanding capital securities) will begin trading a lot more like 30-year bullets, rather than 30-year debt callable in 10-years," Gilligan said.
He added that if banks and corporations cease to issue capital securities in the future, the outstanding securities could also acquire a certain scarcity value.

Passage of the tax legislation also threatens to cut off future supply of bonds with maturities longer than 40 years such as 100-year or "century bonds" recently issued by companies such as Norfolk Southern Corp.

Nanette Abuhoff, senior fixed-income analyst at J.P. Morgan Securities Inc, said that spreads on outstanding century bonds are unlikely to tighten significantly from their current levels, becuase the market has largely anticipated the change. (( -- U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1662 ))
